title: Microsoft MAI coding model becomes the default GitHub Copilot engine by Q4 2026
body: Microsoft used its June 2 Build 2026 keynote to debut an in-house MAI model family that includes a coding-focused model explicitly positioned to power GitHub Copilot, its most direct move yet to reduce dependence on OpenAI for foundation-model capability. One day earlier, on June 1, GitHub flipped every Copilot plan to usage-based billing, replacing flat-rate premium requests with per-token GitHub AI Credits and removing the fallback that let users who exhausted their allowance drop to a cheaper model and keep working. These two events are halves of the same margin story: metered billing now exposes Microsoft's own gross margin on every agentic Copilot request, and a first-party model it does not pay OpenAI per-token for is the cleanest lever to protect that margin. The prediction is that within about two quarters Microsoft makes the MAI coding model the default engine behind GitHub Copilot's high-volume agentic paths — code completion, the autonomous bug/feature/PR agent, and chat — routing GPT-class models to a premium or opt-in tier rather than the standard path. Expect the shift to surface as Copilot release-note or changelog language naming a Microsoft first-party model as the default for Copilot completions or agent mode, distinct per-model token rates in the published GitHub AI Credits price table, and Build/Ignite messaging framing first-party inference as the cost engine under the new metered plans.

summary: Microsoft debuted an in-house MAI coding model at Build 2026 to power GitHub Copilot, a day after GitHub moved Copilot to per-token billing. By Q4 2026 Microsoft makes MAI the default engine for Copilot's high-volume agentic paths, pushing GPT-class models to a premium tier.
